facts.label: legend
facts.quote: Paranormal investigators Ed and Lorraine Warren claimed that Annabelle the Raggedy Ann doll, whose original owners frequently found her in places they hadn't left her, was being used by a demonic spirit in its quest to possess a human soul
facts.text: According to paranormal lore, a student nurse in Connecticut received a cloth doll in 1970 that allegedly shifted positions and moved from room to room on its own.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: The Warrens said a psychic medium had told the student nurse and her roommate that the doll had been taken over by the spirit of a dead seven-year-old girl named Annabelle.
facts.text: The roommates claimed they repeatedly discovered cryptic handwritten notes on parchment paper pleading for help that they believed were written by the doll.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: She was seven years old and her name was Annabelle—Annabelle Higgins.
facts.text: Author Gerald Brittle documented that a medium told the nursing students the doll was inhabited by the spirit of a deceased seven-year-old girl named Annabelle Higgins.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: Its only fatal victim is a visitor who made fun of the doll and then died in a motorcycle accident afterward.
facts.text: Local lore maintains that an occult museum visitor who tapped on the glass case to mock Annabelle died in a fatal motorcycle collision hours later.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Be it known that I, Johnny Gruelle, a citizen of the United States... have invented a new, original, and ornamental Design for Dolls.
facts.source_name: United States Patent and Trademark Office
facts.text: On September 7, 1915, the United States Patent and Trademark Office issued design patent D47789 to cartoonist Johnny Gruelle for the original Raggedy Ann doll.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: What they are really hunting for are anomalies – anything even slightly strange. In the ghost-hunting world, anomaly = ghost. Scientific investigation does not enter into the equation.
facts.text: In 1997, the New England Skeptical Society investigated the Warrens' supernatural case evidence and reported an absence of scientific methodology and empirical validity.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: she now lives in a specially-made demon-proof case marked “Warning: Positively Do Not Open” at the Warren's Occult Museum in Connecticut.
facts.text: Smithsonian Magazine documented in 2015 that the actual Annabelle artifact kept in Connecticut is a mass-manufactured Raggedy Ann cloth doll rather than a creepy porcelain figure.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Skeptical investigators Joe Nickell and Benjamin Radford concluded that the better-known hauntings... did not happen and had been invented.
facts.text: The Committee for Skeptical Inquiry reported that the Warrens systematically relied on unverified personal anecdotes and subjective folklore rather than measurable physical proof.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: The Warrens are good at telling ghost stories... But there's absolutely no reason to believe there is any legitimacy to them.
facts.text: While Ed and Lorraine Warren claimed the doll exerted violent poltergeist activity and inflicted bodily scratches, neurologist Dr. Steven Novella argued that sleep paralysis, power of suggestion, and embellishment fully explain the testimony.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Academics and science writers have dismissed their claims as myth and folklore.
facts.text: Archival searches of Connecticut vital statistics and historical death registries yielded no record of a seven-year-old child named Annabelle Higgins dying in the area.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: she now lives in a specially-made demon-proof case marked “Warning: Positively Do Not Open” at the Warren's Occult Museum in Connecticut.
facts.text: According to occult lore, Ed Warren built a sealed wooden and glass container inscribed with a warning notice after holy water failed to subdue the doll's perceived malice.
